title: A list you keep

prereqs.why: The numbers have to be kept, because three of the four answers are about positions rather than about running totals.
How many there are is not known in advance, which is exactly when a vector earns its place over an array.

statement:
Read integers until the input runs out, keep them, and report:

```
input:   4 -3 9 0 7

output:  size 5
         first 4
         last 7
         middle 9
```

`middle` is the element at index `size / 2`, using integer
division — so for 5 elements it is index 2, and for 4 elements it
is index 2 as well, the first of the two in the middle.

With no input at all:

```
size 0
first none
last none
middle none
```

### The point of the problem

The previous problems streamed: each value was used and thrown
away. These answers are about *positions*, which means the values
have to be kept, and how many there will be is not known until the
end. That is what `std::vector` is for.

```cpp
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> values{};         // empty
values.push_back(x);               // one longer
values.size()                      // how many
values[0]                          // the first
values[values.size() - 1]          // the last
```

A vector grows as you push onto it; you never say how big it will
be. There are named versions of the first and last — `values
.front()` and `values.back()` — which say what they mean and avoid
the `- 1`.

### Constraints

Each number is between -1,000,000 and 1,000,000 and there are at
most 10,000 of them, possibly none.

### Boundary cases

- **No input.** `size()` is 0 and there is no first, last or middle.
  Every one of `values[0]`, `.front()` and `.back()` on an empty
  vector is undefined behaviour, not an error — so the empty case
  has to be checked before any of them is used.
- **One number** is the first, the last, and the middle.
- **An even count**, as in `1 2 3 4`: the middle is index 2, which
  holds 3. Integer division rounds down, which here means the later
  of the two central elements.
- **Two numbers**: `middle` is the second.
hints: Push each number onto a `std::vector<int>` as you read it: `values.push_back(x);` inside the `while (std::cin >> x)` loop.
Check `values.empty()` before touching any element. Indexing an empty vector is undefined behaviour, which may not crash and may quietly print rubbish.
The middle index is `values.size() / 2`. For the first and last, `values.front()` and `values.back()` say what they mean more clearly than `values[0]` and `values[values.size() - 1]`.

cases.expect:
size 0
first none
last none
middle none
